units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Het Steen. Is that the castle?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: What survives is the gateway to a bigger castle.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It was built between 1200 and 1225.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The rest was torn down in the 1800s.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the dark part?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Now we're back in history. It was used as a prison.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: From 1303 to 1827.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: That's more than five hundred years.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Five hundred and twenty-four, if you count it.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: I don't have good sources on who was held there or how they were treated, so I'm not going to make that up.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Good. No invented dungeon.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: There's also an odd carved relief over the archway.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's a figure called Semini. The story is that women once prayed to him for children, and later church people disapproved.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Citizens were even called children of Semini.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Is that real?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The tradition is old. The details, including where the figure came from, are murky.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Call it a local tradition and leave it there.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So three layers at one gate. A real prison, a tangled tradition, and a giant out front.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Right. Take a photo, and then walk up to the cathedral.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Teaser?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In the cathedral, there's a night in 1566 when the church looked like hell.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: That's from a witness.
